nodes.front: Example 4 · Purposeful question: How would you draw a reference triangle in the case where (θ) is greater than 180°?
nodes.back: Listen for: The reference triangle would be drawn for the reference angle of (θ) below the x-axis.

nodes.front: Example 4 · Purposeful question: Why is the sine negative when the terminal point is in Quadrant IV?
nodes.back: Listen for: Quadrant IV is below the x-axis, where all y-values are negative.

nodes.front: Example 4 · Purposeful question: Can more than one angle have the same reference angle?
nodes.back: Listen for: Yes, since the reference angle is the acute angle formed with the x-axis, all angles that have the same angle measure above or below the x-axis would have the same reference angle.

nodes.front: Example 4 · Teacher prompt: What does it mean if a side is opposite (θ)?
nodes.back: Listen for: The side is across from the angle (θ).

nodes.front: Example 4 · Teacher prompt: What does it mean to say a side is adjacent to (θ)?
nodes.back: Listen for: The side is next to the angle (θ) and helps form the angle (θ).

nodes.front: Example 4 · Teacher prompt: Is the hypotenuse opposite or adjacent to (θ)?
nodes.back: Listen for: Adjacent, it is next to the angle (θ) and is one of the lines that helps form the angle (θ).

nodes.front: Example 4 · Teacher prompt: True or False: The hypotenuse is adjacent to the right angle of the reference triangle.
nodes.back: Listen for: False

nodes.front: Example 6 · Connect representations: How does using the unit circle simplify the application of the Pythagorean Identity?
nodes.back: Listen for: The length of the hypotenuse of the reference triangle is always 1, so the square of the hypotenuse is also 1.

nodes.front: Example 6 · Connect representations: How do you determine whether the positive or negative value of the square root is correct when calculating the sine or cosine of (θ)? (1/2)
nodes.back: Listen for: Since the sine is the y-coordinate of the terminal point, it is positive when the terminal point is in Quadrant I or II and negative when it is in Quadrant III or IV.

nodes.front: Example 6 · Connect representations: How do you determine whether the positive or negative value of the square root is correct when calculating the sine or cosine of (θ)? (2/2)
nodes.back: Since the cosine is the x-coordinate of the terminal point, it is positive when the terminal point is in Quadrant I or IV and negative when it is in Quadrant II or III.

nodes.front: Example 6 · Check student thinking: How can you find the cosine when the value of the sine is known?
nodes.back: Listen for: Substitute the value of the sine in the Pythagorean Identity and solve for the cosine. Determine the sign of the cosine by the quadrant in which (θ) is found.

If the coordinates of the terminal point of an angle theta on the unit circle are (-3/5, 4/5), describe and correct the error a student made in finding tan theta. Student work: tan theta = (-3/5)/(4/5) = -3/4.

tan theta = sin theta / cos theta = y/x = (4/5)/(-3/5) = -4/3. The student divided x by y, which is the reciprocal of the tangent (the cotangent). No DOK 3 item exists in the 7-2 TE (item analysis: Examples 1-7, DOK 1 and 2 only; Practice 37 has no printed DOK). …
The graph shows the terminal sides of an angle with measure theta and its supplement, 180 - theta, on the unit circle (terminal points (x, y) in Quadrant I and (?, ?) in Quadrant II).

A. How are the coordinates of the intersection of the terminal side of an angle with measure theta and the unit circle related to the sine and cosine of the angle? (The x-coordinate is the cosine and the y-coordinate is the sine.)
B. What do you notice about theta and the measure of the acute angle formed by the terminal side of 180 - theta and the x-axis? (The acute angles have the same measure.)

C. Draw the terminal sides of angles in Quadrants III and IV that form the same acute angle with the x-axis as the angles in Quadrants I and II. How are these angles related to theta? (180 + theta and 360 - theta.)
D. Communicate Precisely: How are all four terminal sides related geometrically on the coordinate plane? (They are reflections over the coordinate axes.)
What do you notice about the terminal sides of the angles theta and 180 - theta? → They are symmetric about the y-axis.

What do the values of x and y represent when determining the sine and cosine of theta? → The side lengths of a right triangle formed by the x-axis, the line from (x, y) to the origin, and the vertical line from (x, y) to the x-axis.

How are the coordinates of the intersection of the unit circle with the terminal sides of the angles theta and 180 - theta related? → The x-coordinates are the same number with the opposite sign; the y-coordinates are identical.

If theta = 30 degrees, what are the coordinates of the intersection of the unit circle with the terminal sides in each quadrant? → Quadrant I (sqrt3/2, 1/2); Quadrant II (-sqrt3/2, 1/2); Quadrant III (-sqrt3/2, -1/2); Quadrant IV (sqrt3/2, -1/2).

How does the unit circle help to find the values of the sine and cosine of any angle theta? → On the unit circle, the terminal point is (cos theta, sin theta). Off the axes, the reference triangle has hypotenuse 1 and leg lengths |cos theta| and |sin theta|; the quadrant determines the coordinate signs. …
When you connect the four points on the unit circle, the figure is a rectangle. For what angle theta is that rectangle a square? → pi/4, or 45 degrees.
